title: Negative Indices

findings.finding: Negative powers of fractional bases are required without a demonstration of how to simplify the resulting reciprocal fraction.
findings.breakdown: In p9-q16, converting the mixed numeral supplies the fractional base but leaves students to connect the negative-index rule with fraction division. The same unsupported variant recurs in p21-q9-p.
findings.checked: The p3–p4 teaching demonstrates integer bases only. The later p12 review rehearses reciprocals and fraction division, but no teaching demonstrates a negative power of a non-unit fraction. The proposed example gives (5/3)^(-2)=9/25.
findings.assumptions: Mixed-number conversion, ordinary fraction operations and positive powers of fractions are prior knowledge. No calculator is needed.

repair.proposal: Immediately before p9-q16, model: (1 2/3)^(-2)=(5/3)^(-2)=1/((5/3)^2)=1/(25/9)=9/25. Beside the last step state: “Dividing 1 by a fraction gives its reciprocal.” This also prepares students for p21-q9-p; no second demonstration is necessary.

findings.doneWhen: Before q16, students see the negative-index rule applied to an entire fractional base and the resulting fraction division completed.

findings.finding: Parts f and k repeat the unchanged task of evaluating 10^(-3), with no explicit instructional purpose.
findings.breakdown: The later copy provides no new numerical case, representation or comparison.
findings.checked: Both parts have the same expression and share the instruction in p8-q12-root. No retrieval or comparison purpose is stated.
findings.assumptions: The parts are separate practice items.
findings.doneWhen: The later copy uses different values and its answer is updated.

findings.finding: Combined quotient and power-of-power laws with negative exponents are required before their extension to signed exponents is demonstrated.
findings.breakdown: p20-q8 requires subtracting from a negative exponent and then multiplying that exponent by an outer power. Later nested powers also require products of signed exponents. Earlier reciprocal conversions and the single signed-exponent product do not model these decisions.
findings.checked: p3-review-division uses positive input exponents; p12-review-powers-c uses addition of opposite exponents. Neither demonstrates quotient or power-of-power laws with negative input exponents. Independently calculated p20-q8 as 4^(-27), p21-q9-i as 4/25 and p21-q9-r as 1/3.
findings.assumptions: Positive-index laws are prior knowledge from the separately taught index-law material. No calculator is needed.

repair.proposal: Before p20-q8, state that the same-base index laws also apply to negative integer exponents. Model 3^(-2)÷3^4=3^(-2-4)=3^(-6), (3^(-2))^3=3^((-2)×3)=3^(-6), and (3^(-2))^(-1)=3^((-2)×(-1))=3^2.

findings.doneWhen: Students see subtraction and multiplication of signed exponents in the relevant laws before the combined questions.

findings.finding: Connect the two representations of 1/16 already obtained in parts b and c.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up exposes how changing the base changes the exponent while preserving the value.
findings.checked: 4^(-2)=2^(-4), 4^(-3)=2^(-6), and 2^(-8)=4^(-4). These concrete equalities can be established by evaluating powers and using the reciprocal rule.
findings.assumptions: Positive integer powers are prior knowledge.

repair.proposal: Append to p8-q13: i. Using parts b and c, complete 4^(-2)=2^□. Answer: -4. j. Write 4^(-3) as a power of 2. Answer: 2^(-6). k. Write 2^(-8) as a power of 4. Answer: 4^(-4).

findings.doneWhen: The optional follow-up is appended as three separate parts.

findings.finding: Connect the reciprocal values already evaluated in parts d and k.
findings.breakdown: Multiplying these answers links the two negative-index conversion rules.
findings.checked: Part d gives 1/16 and part k gives 16; their product is 1.
findings.assumptions: Multiplication of fractions and the meaning of reciprocal are available by this topic.

repair.proposal: Append optional part u: “Find the product of your answers to parts d and k. Explain why the product is 1.” Expected answer: (1/16)×16=1 because the numbers are reciprocals.

findings.finding: Vary the denominator exponent through negative, zero and positive values while retaining the numerator and base.
findings.breakdown: The sequence distinguishes removing a negative denominator exponent from moving every denominator power into multiplication.
findings.checked: The five answers are 3×2^2, 3×2, 3, 3/2 and 3/(2^2). The unpatterned answer is 7×5^3. All use methods available by this topic.
findings.assumptions: The existing instruction to rewrite with positive indices remains in force.

repair.proposal: After p19-q2-h, add only this instruction: “Predict each answer before rewriting it.” Append i. 3/(2^(-2)); j. 3/(2^(-1)); k. 3/(2^0); l. 3/(2^1); m. 3/(2^2). Expected answers: 3×2^2, 3×2, 3, 3/2, 3/(2^2). Follow with unpatterned part n. 7/(5^(-3)), answer 7×5^3. Only the denominator exponent varies in i–m.

findings.doneWhen: The five-part run and unpatterned follow-up appear under the existing instruction.

findings.finding: Use existing expressions to choose coefficients that make their values equal 1.
findings.breakdown: Students connect the coefficient with the denominator produced by the negative power.
findings.checked: 64 × 4^(-3) = 64/64 = 1 and 25 × 5^(-2) = 25/25 = 1. These use precisely the coefficient and reciprocal method taught in p17 and p18.
findings.assumptions: Optional follow-up to the existing numerical parts.

repair.proposal: Append to p19-q3: i. In part b, replace the coefficient 5 with a number that makes the expression equal 1. Answer: 64. j. In part c, replace the coefficient 7 with a number that makes the expression equal 1. Answer: 25.

findings.doneWhen: The optional parts follow p19-q3-h and each asks for one replacement coefficient.

findings.finding: Extend the supplied power value to products with opposite and neighbouring exponents.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up connects the reciprocal interpretation to multiplication of powers.
findings.checked: 2^10 × 2^(-10) = 1 and 2^10 × 2^(-9) = 2. Students can use the supplied value, reciprocals and the division index law rehearsed in p3-review-division.
findings.assumptions: Optional follow-up using only methods available by the end of this topic.

repair.proposal: Append to p9-q15-root: c. Using 2^10 = 1024, evaluate 2^10 × 2^(-10). Answer: 1. d. Evaluate 2^10 × 2^(-9). Answer: 2.

findings.doneWhen: The two optional parts follow the existing question, with one task per part.

findings.finding: The conversion of 1/(4^3) to a negative power is repeated unchanged without an explicit instructional purpose.
findings.breakdown: The later practice part repeats the complete student task from p10-response-b.
findings.checked: The instructions in p10-rewrite-root and p11-q2-root require the same conversion of the identical expression. Neither states a retrieval or comparison purpose.
findings.assumptions: The earlier identify response is a student task, as shown, rather than a supplied worked demonstration.

repair.proposal: Replace p11-q2-f with 1/(8^3), retaining its instruction. Answer: 8^(-3).

findings.doneWhen: The later copy retains the conversion structure with different values and an updated answer.

findings.finding: Vary the denominator exponent across zero while keeping the base and reciprocal structure fixed.
findings.breakdown: The run connects the two reciprocal laws through the zero exponent.
findings.checked: The proposed expressions equal 4, 2, 1, 1/2 and 1/4 respectively. Both reciprocal laws and the zero-index rule are available. The supplied practice has no equivalent consecutive run.
findings.assumptions: Answers retain positive indices where appropriate under the existing instruction.

repair.proposal: After p14-q2-h, add the single instruction: 'Predict each answer before rewriting it.' Add further parts under the existing instruction: i. 1/(2^(-2)), answer 2^2; j. 1/(2^(-1)), answer 2; k. 1/(2^0), answer 1; l. 1/(2^1), answer 1/2; m. 1/(2^2), answer 1/(2^2). Follow with the unpatterned part n. 1/(5^3), answer 1/(5^3). Only the denominator exponent varies within i–m.

findings.doneWhen: The five-part run and unpatterned follow-up appear under the existing instruction, with only the prediction line added.

findings.finding: Follow the existing product in a denominator by choosing an exponent to obtain a specified value.
findings.breakdown: Students reverse the same exponent addition and reciprocal operations used in the original task.
findings.checked: 1/(7^(-3) × 7^n) = 7^(3-n), giving n = 3 for a value of 1 and n = 2 for a value of 7. Both can be found using the taught index laws without logarithms.
findings.assumptions: Optional numerical follow-up; no general proof is requested.

repair.proposal: Append optional parts to p14-q6: a. Find n so that 1/(7^(-3) × 7^n) = 1. Answer: n = 3. b. Find n so that 1/(7^(-3) × 7^n) = 7. Answer: n = 2.

findings.doneWhen: Each appended part asks for one exponent using the existing base and denominator structure.

findings.finding: Parts b and l repeat the unchanged task of evaluating 1/(5^3), with no explicit instructional purpose.
findings.breakdown: The later copy adds no new numerical case or comparison within the mixed exercise.
findings.checked: Both expressions and their shared instruction are identical. Mixed practice explains the choice between representations but supplies no explicit purpose for this exact repetition.
findings.doneWhen: The later copy uses different values and its answer is updated.

findings.finding: The review omits multiplication of equal-base powers, zero indices and division by a fraction, all substantial steps in the introductory derivations.
findings.breakdown: The first derivation requires combining exponents and evaluating 5^0; the second requires replacing division by a fraction with multiplication by its reciprocal. Identifying a reciprocal does not rehearse the division operation.
findings.checked: Neither p12 review block rehearses these operations. The immediately preceding topic's teaching and p11-q4 do not rehearse them. The zero-index review on p3 is earlier and does not meet the immediately preceding review exception.
findings.assumptions: These are prior skills from Index Laws and Operations with Fractions and Decimals. No calculator is needed.

repair.proposal: Append three short rows: (1) Simplify using the multiplication index law: 5^2 × 5^3; 3^4 × 3. (2) Evaluate: 5^0; 7^0. (3) Simplify: 1 ÷ (1/5); 2 ÷ (1/3). Expected answers: 5^5, 3^5; 1, 1; 5, 6. These six short items fit alongside the existing review within one page.

findings.doneWhen: The opening review rehearses each operation before the two derivations.

findings.finding: The coefficient topic has no opening review rehearsing multiplication of a whole number by a unit fraction.
findings.breakdown: The introductory examples require students to combine expressions such as 4 × (1/3^2) into 4/3^2 while learning which factor the negative index affects.
findings.checked: p17-positive-demonstrations uses this fraction operation directly. Neither the immediately preceding mixed practice nor the p12 review rehearses multiplication by a unit fraction. Positive-power evaluation is removed from the candidate because p16-q5 repeatedly rehearses it.
findings.assumptions: Ordinary fraction multiplication is prior knowledge from Operations with Fractions and Decimals. No calculator is needed.

repair.proposal: Before p17-laws-block, add: Write as a single fraction: (a) 3 × 1/8, (b) 4 × 1/9, (c) 7 × 1/25. Expected answers: 3/8, 4/9, 7/25.

findings.doneWhen: A short opening review rehearses multiplication by a unit fraction before the coefficient examples.

protectedGroups.observation: Swapping 73 and 12 distinguishes the roles of base and exponent.
protectedGroups.varies: Which number is the base and which is the exponent.
protectedGroups.invariant: The two numbers, unit numerator and reciprocal-to-negative-power conversion.

protectedGroups.observation: The base stays unchanged while the denominator's exponent becomes negative, including the implicit exponent 1.
protectedGroups.invariant: Base 2, unit numerator and conversion direction.

protectedGroups.observation: The reciprocal conversion works for exponent magnitude 1 and for a larger magnitude.
protectedGroups.invariant: Base 2, conversion direction and instruction not to evaluate.

protectedGroups.observation: A larger exponent magnitude changes the exponent in the denominator without changing the conversion.
A negative exponent in the denominator becomes the corresponding positive exponent in the numerator.
A negative power and its reciprocal require different positive-power forms; the final pair reverses their order.
protectedGroups.varies: Within each pair, whether the negative power is itself the expression or is in the denominator.
protectedGroups.invariant: Base and exponent within each pair, and the instruction not to evaluate.

protectedGroups.observation: Matched reciprocal pairs reinforce choosing the conversion from the expression's structure.
protectedGroups.varies: Position of the negative power within each pair.
protectedGroups.invariant: Base and exponent magnitude within each pair.

protectedGroups.observation: Decreasing the exponent by one divides the value by five, continuing through zero into negative exponents.
The reciprocal relationship persists across bases, and exponent -2 squares the denominator.
protectedGroups.invariant: Corresponding base order and reciprocal structure. The repeated base-5 entries connect these comparisons to the first column.

protectedGroups.observation: Each table continues the same multiplicative pattern across exponent zero.
protectedGroups.varies: Exponent within each table and base between tables.

protectedGroups.observation: The sign depends on the parity of the power and on whether a minus sign lies outside the power.
protectedGroups.varies: Exponent and presence of an external minus sign.

protectedGroups.observation: Successive powers and their reciprocals have opposite exponents.
protectedGroups.varies: Magnitude of the exponent from 2 to 4.

protectedGroups.observation: Swapping the base and exponent reinforces that their roles remain distinct and that neither power needs evaluating.
protectedGroups.varies: The positions of 35 and 67 as base and exponent magnitude.
protectedGroups.invariant: A unit numerator and a negative power in the denominator, rewritten as a positive power.

protectedGroups.observation: Changing the exponent changes only the denominator power; the coefficient remains unchanged.
Reverse conversion retains the numerator and base while changing the exponent's sign.
The numerator remains a coefficient; a minus in the numerator or outside the fraction has the same effect.
protectedGroups.varies: Numerator value, sign and placement of the minus sign.

protectedGroups.observation: Changing the coefficient's sign does not change the negative power.
The denominator base becomes the multiplication base unchanged.
The numerator sign survives denominator conversion.
Changing the coefficient changes the resulting numerator only.

dropped.reason: The mathematics and instruction pass, but its denominator-exponent comparison substantially overlaps c12. Under the four-suggestion limit, retain c12 because it also exposes preservation of the coefficient, alongside the three concrete extensions.

candidates.finding: Add a run that crosses zero in the denominator exponent while retaining the same base.
